narrations: Welcome to Episode 2 of Hello World, pg_bio! In Episode 1, we treated DNA and proteins as 1D strings. But in reality, a protein folds into a 3D molecular machine where catalysis happens inside a 4-Angstrom binding pocket.
Normally, finding which atoms sit inside a 3D sphere requires pulling millions of coordinates into Python and building an in-memory KD-tree or running brute-force Pythagorean distance loops.

pg_bio solves this with Morton coding—also known as a Z-Order space-filling curve. Our Rust function z_order_encode interleaves the bits of X, Y, and Z coordinates into a single 64-bit integer. That means a standard 1D PostgreSQL B-Tree index now acts as a 3D spatial bounding box!
Even better, once the B-Tree narrows down the pocket atoms, theozyme_rmsd runs a zero-allocation 3-by-3 Jacobi SVD right inside SQL to rotationally align the catalytic metal and nucleophilic water.
That is 3D structural biology powered by B-Trees and linear algebra inside PostgreSQL. Visit ideia dot me and the pg_bio GitHub repo to try the interactive 3D notebooks.
